Commentary of Ibn Kathir (Tafsir al-Quran al-'Azim) on surah 105, verse 1–5 (part 1 of 3):

Tafsir of Surat al-Fil (The Elephant)
It is a Meccan surah.
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
* *
This is one of the blessings with which Allah favoured the Quraysh, in that He turned away from them the People of the Elephant, who had resolved to demolish the Ka'bah and erase its trace from existence. So Allah destroyed them, humbled their noses, frustrated their endeavour, misguided their deeds, and returned them in the worst state of failure. They were a Christian people, and their religion at that time was closer to the truth than the idol worship in which the Quraysh were engaged. Yet this was by way of irhas (a preparatory sign) and tawti'ah (a paving of the way) for the mission of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for he was born in that year according to the most well-known opinions. The state of the decree (qadar) seems to say: "We did not give you victory, O assembly of Quraysh, over the Abyssinians because of your superiority over them, but to protect the Ancient House, which We will honour, exalt and revere through the mission of the unlettered Prophet Muhammad, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, the Seal of the Prophets."

This is the story of the People of the Elephant in a summarised, concise and brief manner. It has already been mentioned in the story of the People of the Trench (ukhdud) [[At the commentary on verse 4 of Surat al-Buruj.]] that Dhu Nuwas, who was the last of the kings of Himyar and was a polytheist, was the one who killed the People of the Trench, who were Christians, and they numbered nearly twenty thousand. None of them escaped except Dawas Dhu Tha'labān, who went and sought help from Caesar, the king of Syria, who was a Christian. He wrote to the Negus, the king of Abyssinia, on his behalf, since he was closer to them. So he sent with him two commanders: Ariyat and Abraha ibn al-Sabbah, Abu Yaksum [[In the manuscript A: "Abu Bakshum".]], with a dense army. They entered Yemen, roamed through its lands, and seized the kingdom from Himyar, and Dhu Nuwas perished by drowning in the sea. The Abyssinians established their rule over Yemen, and these two commanders were over them: Ariyat and Abraha. They disagreed about their affairs, contended, fought and drew up their lines against each other. One of them said to the other: "There is no need for the two armies to clash between us, but come out to me and I will come out to you. Whichever of us kills the other will then hold the kingdom alone." The other agreed to that, and they fought in single combat, each holding a spear. Ariyat charged at Abraha and struck him with the sword, slitting his nose and mouth and splitting his face. Atwadah, the mawla of Abraha, charged at Ariyat and killed him, and Abraha returned wounded. He treated his wound and it healed, and he took sole charge of the Abyssinian army in Yemen. The Negus wrote to him rebuking him for what he had done, threatening him and swearing that he would certainly trample his land and cut off his forelock. Abraha sent to him seeking to soften his heart and to win him over, and he sent with his messenger gifts and presents, and a leather bag containing soil from Yemen, and he had cut off his forelock and sent it with him. He wrote in his letter: "Let the king tread upon this bag so that he may fulfil his oath, and this is my forelock, which I have sent to you." When that reached him, it pleased him, he was content with him, and he confirmed him in his post. Abraha sent to the Negus saying: "I will build for you a church in the land of Yemen, the like of which has never been built before." So he began to build a vast church in San'a, high in its construction, lofty in its courtyard, and adorned in its surroundings. The Arabs named it al-Qulleys because of its height, for the one who looks at it nearly has his cap fall from his head because of the height of its building. Abraha al-Ashram resolved to divert the Hajj of the Arabs to it, just as the Hajj is performed to the Ka'bah in Mecca, and he proclaimed this throughout his kingdom. The Arabs, both the 'Adnani and the Qahtani, disliked that, and the Quraysh were greatly angered by it, to the extent that some of them went to it and managed to enter it by night. They defiled it and then returned. When the custodians (sadanah) saw that act of defilement, they reported the matter to their king Abraha and said to him: "Only some of the Quraysh did this, out of anger for their House which you have sought to rival with this one." So Abraha swore that he would certainly march to the House in Mecca and destroy it stone by stone.

Muqatil ibn Sulayman mentioned that some young men of the Quraysh entered it and kindled a fire inside it, and on a day when there was a strong wind, the fire spread and burnt it, and it collapsed to the ground.

So Abraha prepared himself for this, and set out with a dense, mighty army, so that no one could repel him from it. He took with him a great elephant of enormous body, the like of which had never been seen, called Mahmud, which the Negus, king of Abyssinia, had sent to him for this purpose. It is said that there were also eight elephants with him, and it is said twelve elephants, and other figures were said, and Allah knows best. He intended to demolish the Ka'bah with it, by placing chains on the corners and putting them round the elephant's neck, then driving it so that it would knock down the wall all at once. When the Arabs heard of his march, they were greatly alarmed, and they considered it their duty to defend the House and to repel whoever intended to harm it with evil. A man from the nobles and kings of the people of Yemen, called "Dhu Nafr," went out to him and called his people and whoever among the other Arabs answered him to fight Abraha and to strive in the cause of the House of Allah, against what he intended of its demolition and ruin. They responded to him and fought Abraha, but he defeated them, because of what Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, willed of the honour and exaltation of the House. Dhu Nafr was captured and Abraha kept him with him. Then he proceeded on his way until, when he reached the land of Khath'am, Nufayl ibn Habib al-Khath'ami confronted him with his people, Shahran and Nahis, and they fought him, but Abraha defeated them, and Nufayl ibn Habib was captured. He intended to kill him, then pardoned him, and kept him with him to guide him through the lands of the Hijaz. When he drew near the land of al-Ta'if, its people, Thaqif, came out to him and gave him gifts out of fear for their House that they had there, which they called al-Lat. So he honoured them, and they sent with him Abu Righal as a guide. When Abraha reached al-Mughammas, which is near Mecca, he halted there, and his army raided the camels and other livestock of the people of Mecca, and they seized them. Among the herd were two hundred camels belonging to Abd al-Muttalib. The one who raided the herd on Abraha's orders was the commander of the vanguard, who was called "al-Aswad ibn Maqsud." Some of the Arabs satirised him, as reported by Ibn Ishaq [[See: al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah of Ibn Hisham (1/51).]]. Abraha sent Hunatah al-Himyari to Mecca and ordered him to bring him the noblest of the Quraysh, and to inform them that the king had not come to fight them unless they tried to repel him from the House. Hunatah came and was directed to Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim, and he conveyed to him what Abraha had said. Abd al-Muttalib said to him: "By Allah, we do not wish to fight him, and we have no power for that. This is the Sacred House of Allah and the House of His friend Abraham. If He protects it from him, then it is His House and His sanctuary, and if He leaves him to it, then by Allah we have no defence against him." Hunatah said to him: "Then go with me to him." So he went with him, and when Abraha saw him he held him in great honour, for Abd al-Muttalib was a handsome man of fine appearance. Abraha got down from his throne and sat with him on the carpet, and said to his interpreter: "Say to him: What is your need?" Abd al-Muttalib said to the interpreter: "My need is that the king return to me the two hundred camels that he has taken from me." Abraha said to his interpreter: "Say to him: You had impressed me when I saw you, but now I have lost my regard for you since you spoke to me. Do you speak to me about two hundred camels that I have taken from you, and leave aside a House which is your religion and the religion of your fathers, and which I have come to demolish, and you do not speak to me about it?" Abd al-Muttalib said to him: "I am the lord of the camels, and the House has a Lord who will protect it." He said: "He would not be able to prevent me!" He said: "You and that."

It is also said that a group of the noble Arabs went with Abd al-Muttalib, and they offered Abraha a third of the wealth of Tihamah on condition that he turn back from the House, but he refused them. Abraha returned to Abd al-Muttalib his camels. Abd al-Muttalib returned to the Quraysh and ordered them to leave Mecca and take refuge on the mountaintops, out of fear for them from the harm of the army. Then Abd al-Muttalib stood, took hold of the ring of the door of the Ka'bah, and with him stood a group of the Quraysh, calling upon Allah and seeking His help against Abraha and his army. Abd al-Muttalib said, while holding the ring of the door of the Ka'bah:

"O Allah, indeed a man defends his camp,
So defend Your sanctuary.
Let their cross not overcome
And their stratagem against Your might, tomorrow, not prevail."

Ibn Ishaq said: Then Abd al-Muttalib released the ring of the door, and they went out to the mountaintops [[See: al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah of Ibn Hisham (1/52).]].

Muqatil ibn Sulayman mentioned that they left near the House a hundred garlanded camels, perhaps some of the army would take something from them unjustly, and Allah would take vengeance on him.

When Abraha woke in the morning, he prepared to enter Mecca. He readied his elephant, which was named Mahmud, and arrayed his army. When they turned the elephant towards Mecca, Nufayl ibn Habib came and stood beside it, then took hold of its ear and said: "Kneel down, Mahmud, and return safely from where you came, for you are in the land of Allah the Sacred." Then he let go of its ear, and the elephant knelt down. Nufayl ibn Habib ran off until he climbed up the mountain. They struck the elephant to make it stand, but it refused. They struck it on the head with an iron implement and inserted their hooks into its flanks and pricked it with them to make it stand, but it refused. They turned it back towards Yemen and it got up and trotted; they turned it towards Syria and it did the same; they turned it towards the east and it did the same; and when they turned it towards Mecca it knelt down. Allah sent upon them birds from the sea, like swallows and sparrows. With each bird were three stones it carried: one stone in its beak and two in its feet, like chickpeas and lentils. They did not strike any of them without destroying them, though not all of them were struck. They fled in all directions, rushing along the road and asking about Nufayl to guide them along this path. Nufayl was on the top of the mountain with the Quraysh and the Arabs of the Hijaz, looking at what vengeance Allah had sent upon the People of the Elephant. Nufayl kept saying: "Where is the escape? The God is the Seeker, and the Ashram is the defeated, not the victor."

Ibn Ishaq said: Nufayl also said in this:

"Ah, may Rudayna greet us, may our eyes be bright at dawn,
Rudayna, if you had seen, and you did not see, by the side of al-Muhassab, what we saw,
Then you would have excused me and praised my course, and you would not have grieved over what had passed between us.
I praised Allah when I saw the birds, and feared the stones that would be thrown upon us.
Every people asks about Nufayl, as if I owed a debt to the Habashah!"

After it is related, with its chains of transmission, that Al-Waqidi said: when they had prepared themselves to enter the Haram (the Sacred Precinct of Makkah) and had readied the elephant, they could not turn it toward any direction other than the Haram, but whichever direction they turned it, it went. When they turned it toward the Haram, it knelt down and cried out. Abraha began to attack the elephant's handler, shouting at him and beating him, so as to force the elephant to enter the Haram. The matter dragged on.

Meanwhile, Abd al-Muttalib and a group of the nobles of Makkah, among them al-Mut'im ibn 'Adi, 'Amr ibn 'A'idh ibn 'Imran ibn Makhzum, and Mas'ud [ibn 'Amr] al-Thaqafi, were on Hira' watching what the Abyssinians were doing and what would befall them concerning the matter of the elephant, which was a wondrous and marvellous thing. While they were in this state, Allah sent against them birds in flocks (ababil), meaning in separate groups, yellow, unlike pigeons, with red feet. Each bird carried three stones. They came and hovered over them and released those stones upon them, and they were destroyed.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: They brought two elephants. One of them, Mahmud, knelt down, while the other became obstinate and was pelted with stones.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: They had a number of elephants with them. Mahmud, which was the king's elephant, knelt down so that the rest of the elephants would follow its example. Among them was an elephant that became obstinate and was pelted, and the rest of the elephants then fled.

'Ata' ibn Yasar and others said: Not all of them were struck by the punishment at that very moment. Some of them perished swiftly, and some began to fall apart limb by limb while they were fleeing. Abraha was among those who fell apart limb by limb, until he died in the lands of Khath'am.

Ibn Ishaq said: They set out, falling apart along every road and perishing at every watering place. Abraha was afflicted in his body, and they carried him with them, while his fingers dropped off one joint at a time, until they brought him to Sana'a, and he was like a young bird. He did not die until his chest split open from his heart, so they claim.

Muqatil ibn Sulayman mentioned that the Quraysh obtained a great deal of wealth from their spoils and from what was with them, and that Abd al-Muttalib that day acquired so much gold that it filled a pit.

Ibn Ishaq said: Ya'qub ibn 'Utba informed me that it was related to him that the first time measles and smallpox were seen in the land of the Arabs was in that year, and that the first time bitter herbs, colocynth, and 'ushr [a bitter plant] were seen was also that year.

[Editor's note: see Ibn Hisham's Sirah (1/54).]

The same is related from 'Ikrimah, through a sound route.

Ibn Ishaq said: When Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ), among the blessings and favours He reminded the Quraysh of was what He had averted from them of the affair of the Abyssinians, so that their affairs and their period [of prosperity] might endure. He said: ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant? Did He not make their plot go astray? And He sent against them birds in flocks, striking them with stones of baked clay, and He made them like chewed-up straw.﴾ ﴿For the security of the Quraysh, their security in the caravans of winter and summer, let them worship the Lord of this House, who has fed them against hunger and secured them against fear.﴾ [Surah Quraysh]. That is, so that He would not change anything of their condition in which they were, because of the good Allah wished for them, had they accepted it.

Ibn Hisham said: The ababil are groups, and the Arabs do not use a singular form for them. He said: As for sijjil, Yunus the grammarian and Abu 'Ubayda informed me that among the Arabs it means "hard and firm." He said: Some of the exegetes mentioned that they are two words in Persian, which the Arabs made into one word; it is actually sanj and gil. By sanj is meant stone, and by gil, clay. The meaning is: stones of these two kinds, stone and clay. He said: The 'asf is the leaf of the crop that has not been cut, its singular being 'asfah. End of what he mentioned.

[Editor's note: see Ibn Hisham's Sirah (1/55).]

Hammad ibn Salamah related from 'Asim, from Zirr, from 'Abd Allah, and Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, regarding ﴿birds in flocks﴾ that he said: "al-Faraq" [the separate groups].

Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: ababil means that some of them follow others. Al-Hasan al-Basri and Qatadah said: ababil means many. Mujahid said: ababil means scattered, consecutive, and gathered together. Ibn Zayd said: ababil means varied, coming from here and from there; they came to them from every place.

Al-Kisa'i said: I heard the grammarians saying: ubul is like 'ujul [calves]. He said: I have also heard some grammarians say: the singular of ababil is ibil.

Ibn Jarir said: [Ibn al-Muthanna related to us]: 'Abd al-A'la related to me, Dawud related to me, from Ishaq ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith ibn Nawfal, that he said regarding His saying ﴿and He sent against them birds in flocks﴾: they are groups, like herds of camels.

Abu Kurayb related to us: Waki' related to us, from Ibn 'Awn, from Ibn Sirin, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿and He sent against them birds in flocks﴾ that he said: They had beaks like the beaks of birds and paws like the paws of dogs.

Ya'qub related to us: Hushaym related to us: Husayn informed us, from 'Ikrimah regarding His saying ﴿birds in flocks﴾ that he said: They were green birds that came out of the sea, having heads like the heads of beasts of prey.

Ibn Bashshar related to us: Ibn Mahdi related to us, from Sufyan, from al-A'mash, from Abu Sufyan, from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr regarding ﴿birds in flocks﴾ that he said: They are sea birds, black, with stones in their beaks and talons.

These are sound chains of transmission.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: They were green birds with yellow beaks, moving among them.

From Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and 'Ata': the ababil birds were like those called the mythical "'Anqa' Mughrib." This was related from them by Ibn Abi Hatim.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: Abu Zur'ah related to us: 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Shaybah related to us: Abu Mu'awiyah related to us, from al-A'mash, from Abu Sufyan, from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, who said: When Allah wished to destroy the companions of the elephant, He sent against them birds created from the sea, like swallows. Each bird carried three stones, speckled: two stones in its feet and one stone in its beak. He said: They came and lined up over their heads, then they screamed and dropped what was in their feet and beaks. No stone fell on a man's head without coming out of his anus, and none fell on any part of his body without coming out the other side. Allah sent a strong wind that struck the stones and increased their force, and they were all destroyed.

As for al-Suddi, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿stones of baked clay﴾: he said: clay in stones, "sank wa-kil" [two Persian words for stone and clay]. We have already presented the explanation of this, which suffices here without repetition.

* *

As for His saying ﴿and He made them like chewed-up straw﴾: Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it means the chaff that common people call hubur. In another report from Sa'id: the leaves of wheat. He also said: the 'asf is chaff, and al-ma'kul is the young green crop cut for animals. Al-Hasan al-Basri said the same.

From Ibn 'Abbas: the 'asf is the husk that is over the grain, like the covering over wheat.

Ibn Zayd said: the 'asf is the leaves of the crop and the leaves of herbs when animals eat them and then drop them as dung, and it becomes crumbled.

The meaning is: Allah, glorified and exalted, destroyed them and annihilated them, and turned them back with their scheming and their rage, without gaining any good. He destroyed most of them, and none of them returned with anything good except wounded, as happened to their king Abraha, whose chest split open from his heart when he reached his city of Sana'a. He informed them of what had happened to them, and then he died. His son Yaksum then ruled after him, then after him his brother Masruq ibn Abraha [ruled].

[Editor's note: see Ibn Hisham's Sirah (1/61–62).]

Then Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan al-Himyari went to Khosrow [the Persian king] seeking his help against the Abyssinians, and he sent with him troops from his armies, who fought alongside him. Allah restored to them their kingdom and what their forefathers had possessed of kingship, and delegations of the Arabs came to him to congratulate him.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr related to us, from 'Amrah bint 'Abd al-Rahman ibn As'ad ibn Zurarah, from 'A'ishah, who said: I saw the elephant's driver and its handler in Makkah, both blind and crippled, begging for food.

[Editor's note: see Ibn Hisham's Sirah (1/57).] Al-Waqidi related the same from 'A'ishah, and he also related from Asma' bint Abi Bakr that she said: they were both crippled, begging people for food, near Isaf and Na'ilah, where the polytheists slaughter their sacrifices.

I say: the name of the elephant's driver was Unays.

The hafiz Abu Nu'aym mentioned in his book Dala'il al-Nubuwwah, through the route of Ibn Wahb, from Ibn Lahi'ah, from 'Uqayl ibn Khalid, from 'Uthman ibn al-Mughirah, the story of the companions of the elephant. He did not mention that Abraha came from Yemen, but rather that he appointed over the army a man called Shamar ibn Maksud, and the army was twenty thousand strong. He mentioned that the birds attacked them at night, and in the morning they were lying dead.

This narrative is very strange, although Abu Nu'aym strengthened it and preferred it over others. The correct account is that Abraha al-Ashram al-Habashi came to Makkah, as the narratives and the poetry indicate. Likewise Ibn Lahi'ah related from al-Aswad, from 'Urwah, that Abraha sent al-Aswad ibn Maksud over a battalion with the elephant, and he did not mention Abraha's own coming. The correct view is that he came, and perhaps Ibn Maksud was at the head of the army. And Allah knows best.

Then Ibn Ishaq related some of the poetry of the Arabs concerning the story of the companions of the elephant. Among it is the poetry of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Za'bari:

They drew back from the heart of Makkah, for it
Was of old a sanctuary never to be violated...
The Shi'ra [star] was not created on the nights it was made sacred,
When no mighty one among mankind would seek it...
Ask the commander of the army what he saw of it?
For he will surely be told of its fate by the ignorant...
Sixty thousand did not return to their land,
Nor did the sick among them survive after their return...
'Ad and Jurhum had dwelt there before them,
And Allah above His servants keeps it secure...

[Editor's note: see Ibn Hisham's Sirah (1/58).]

Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat al-Ansari al-Mari [in some copies: al-Madani] said:
And of their doing on the day of the elephant of al-Habush,
When everything they brought was a cluster of crowded ones...
Their goads beneath its flanks,
And they had slit its nose, so it was torn...
They made its whip a lash,
When they turned it, its back was wounded...
So it turned back, retreating along its path,
And whoever was there had earned injustice...
Then He sent upon them from above a stone-storm
That wrapped them up like a sack of ... [a crowd]...
Their rabbis urged them to patience,
While they bleated like the bleating of sheep...

Abu al-Salt ibn Abi Rabi'ah al-Thaqafi said, and it is also attributed to Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt ibn Abi Rabi'ah:
Indeed the signs of our Lord are lasting,
None disputes them except the ungrateful...
The night and the day were created, and each
Has a reckoning that is clear and decreed...
Then a merciful Lord reveals the day
With a sun whose rays are spread out...
The elephant was held back at al-Mughammas until
It began to crawl, as if it were struck down...
Its neck was bound to the ground, as if it had been cut
From the back of a steep hill...
Around it were champions of the kings of Kindah,
Hard in war, like falcons...
They left it behind, then all of them fled,
All their shin bones broken.

Every religion on the Day of Resurrection with Allah ... is ruined, except the religion of the Hanifiyyah (the pure monotheism of Abraham) ...

I have already mentioned in the commentary on Surah al-Fath that on the day of al-Hudaybiyyah, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came into view at the mountain pass that descends to the Quraysh, his camel knelt down. They urged her on, but she refused to rise. They said, "al-Qaswa has become stubborn," meaning she had balked. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "al-Qaswa has not become stubborn, nor is that her habit, but the one who restrained the elephant has restrained her." Then he said, "By Him in whose hand is my soul, they will not ask me today for any arrangement in which they honour the sacred things of Allah, except that I will agree to it." Then he urged her on and she got up. The hadith is related by al-Bukhari alone [[The takhrij of this hadith was mentioned under the commentary on verse 26 of Surah al-Fath, and it is in Sahih al-Bukhari, nos. (2731, 2732).]].

In the two Sahihs (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim) it is reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said on the day of the Conquest of Makkah: "Allah withheld the elephant from Makkah and gave His Messenger and the believers power over it. Its sanctity has returned today as it was yesterday. So let the one who is present convey it to the one who is absent" [[Sahih al-Bukhari, no. (112), and Sahih Muslim, no. (1355), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]].

End of the commentary on Surah al-Fil.

Commentary of Ibn Kathir (Tafsir al-Quran al-'Azim) on surah 105, verse 1–5 (part 1 of 3):

Tafsir of Surat al-Fil (The Elephant)
It is a Meccan surah.
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
* *
This is one of the blessings with which Allah favoured the Quraysh, in that He turned away from them the People of the Elephant, who had resolved to demolish the Ka'bah and erase its trace from existence. So Allah destroyed them, humbled their noses, frustrated their endeavour, misguided their deeds, and returned them in the worst state of failure. They were a Christian people, and their religion at that time was closer to the truth than the idol worship in which the Quraysh were engaged. Yet this was by way of irhas (a preparatory sign) and tawti'ah (a paving of the way) for the mission of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for he was born in that year according to the most well-known opinions. The state of the decree (qadar) seems to say: "We did not give you victory, O assembly of Quraysh, over the Abyssinians because of your superiority over them, but to protect the Ancient House, which We will honour, exalt and revere through the mission of the unlettered Prophet Muhammad, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, the Seal of the Prophets."

This is the story of the People of the Elephant in a summarised, concise and brief manner. It has already been mentioned in the story of the People of the Trench (ukhdud) [[At the commentary on verse 4 of Surat al-Buruj.]] that Dhu Nuwas, who was the last of the kings of Himyar and was a polytheist, was the one who killed the People of the Trench, who were Christians, and they numbered nearly twenty thousand. None of them escaped except Dawas Dhu Tha'labān, who went and sought help from Caesar, the king of Syria, who was a Christian. He wrote to the Negus, the king of Abyssinia, on his behalf, since he was closer to them. So he sent with him two commanders: Ariyat and Abraha ibn al-Sabbah, Abu Yaksum [[In the manuscript A: "Abu Bakshum".]], with a dense army. They entered Yemen, roamed through its lands, and seized the kingdom from Himyar, and Dhu Nuwas perished by drowning in the sea. The Abyssinians established their rule over Yemen, and these two commanders were over them: Ariyat and Abraha. They disagreed about their affairs, contended, fought and drew up their lines against each other. One of them said to the other: "There is no need for the two armies to clash between us, but come out to me and I will come out to you. Whichever of us kills the other will then hold the kingdom alone." The other agreed to that, and they fought in single combat, each holding a spear. Ariyat charged at Abraha and struck him with the sword, slitting his nose and mouth and splitting his face. Atwadah, the mawla of Abraha, charged at Ariyat and killed him, and Abraha returned wounded. He treated his wound and it healed, and he took sole charge of the Abyssinian army in Yemen. The Negus wrote to him rebuking him for what he had done, threatening him and swearing that he would certainly trample his land and cut off his forelock. Abraha sent to him seeking to soften his heart and to win him over, and he sent with his messenger gifts and presents, and a leather bag containing soil from Yemen, and he had cut off his forelock and sent it with him. He wrote in his letter: "Let the king tread upon this bag so that he may fulfil his oath, and this is my forelock, which I have sent to you." When that reached him, it pleased him, he was content with him, and he confirmed him in his post. Abraha sent to the Negus saying: "I will build for you a church in the land of Yemen, the like of which has never been built before." So he began to build a vast church in San'a, high in its construction, lofty in its courtyard, and adorned in its surroundings. The Arabs named it al-Qulleys because of its height, for the one who looks at it nearly has his cap fall from his head because of the height of its building. Abraha al-Ashram resolved to divert the Hajj of the Arabs to it, just as the Hajj is performed to the Ka'bah in Mecca, and he proclaimed this throughout his kingdom. The Arabs, both the 'Adnani and the Qahtani, disliked that, and the Quraysh were greatly angered by it, to the extent that some of them went to it and managed to enter it by night. They defiled it and then returned. When the custodians (sadanah) saw that act of defilement, they reported the matter to their king Abraha and said to him: "Only some of the Quraysh did this, out of anger for their House which you have sought to rival with this one." So Abraha swore that he would certainly march to the House in Mecca and destroy it stone by stone.

Muqatil ibn Sulayman mentioned that some young men of the Quraysh entered it and kindled a fire inside it, and on a day when there was a strong wind, the fire spread and burnt it, and it collapsed to the ground.

So Abraha prepared himself for this, and set out with a dense, mighty army, so that no one could repel him from it. He took with him a great elephant of enormous body, the like of which had never been seen, called Mahmud, which the Negus, king of Abyssinia, had sent to him for this purpose. It is said that there were also eight elephants with him, and it is said twelve elephants, and other figures were said, and Allah knows best. He intended to demolish the Ka'bah with it, by placing chains on the corners and putting them round the elephant's neck, then driving it so that it would knock down the wall all at once. When the Arabs heard of his march, they were greatly alarmed, and they considered it their duty to defend the House and to repel whoever intended to harm it with evil. A man from the nobles and kings of the people of Yemen, called "Dhu Nafr," went out to him and called his people and whoever among the other Arabs answered him to fight Abraha and to strive in the cause of the House of Allah, against what he intended of its demolition and ruin. They responded to him and fought Abraha, but he defeated them, because of what Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, willed of the honour and exaltation of the House. Dhu Nafr was captured and Abraha kept him with him. Then he proceeded on his way until, when he reached the land of Khath'am, Nufayl ibn Habib al-Khath'ami confronted him with his people, Shahran and Nahis, and they fought him, but Abraha defeated them, and Nufayl ibn Habib was captured. He intended to kill him, then pardoned him, and kept him with him to guide him through the lands of the Hijaz. When he drew near the land of al-Ta'if, its people, Thaqif, came out to him and gave him gifts out of fear for their House that they had there, which they called al-Lat. So he honoured them, and they sent with him Abu Righal as a guide. When Abraha reached al-Mughammas, which is near Mecca, he halted there, and his army raided the camels and other livestock of the people of Mecca, and they seized them. Among the herd were two hundred camels belonging to Abd al-Muttalib. The one who raided the herd on Abraha's orders was the commander of the vanguard, who was called "al-Aswad ibn Maqsud." Some of the Arabs satirised him, as reported by Ibn Ishaq [[See: al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah of Ibn Hisham (1/51).]]. Abraha sent Hunatah al-Himyari to Mecca and ordered him to bring him the noblest of the Quraysh, and to inform them that the king had not come to fight them unless they tried to repel him from the House. Hunatah came and was directed to Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim, and he conveyed to him what Abraha had said. Abd al-Muttalib said to him: "By Allah, we do not wish to fight him, and we have no power for that. This is the Sacred House of Allah and the House of His friend Abraham. If He protects it from him, then it is His House and His sanctuary, and if He leaves him to it, then by Allah we have no defence against him." Hunatah said to him: "Then go with me to him." So he went with him, and when Abraha saw him he held him in great honour, for Abd al-Muttalib was a handsome man of fine appearance. Abraha got down from his throne and sat with him on the carpet, and said to his interpreter: "Say to him: What is your need?" Abd al-Muttalib said to the interpreter: "My need is that the king return to me the two hundred camels that he has taken from me." Abraha said to his interpreter: "Say to him: You had impressed me when I saw you, but now I have lost my regard for you since you spoke to me. Do you speak to me about two hundred camels that I have taken from you, and leave aside a House which is your religion and the religion of your fathers, and which I have come to demolish, and you do not speak to me about it?" Abd al-Muttalib said to him: "I am the lord of the camels, and the House has a Lord who will protect it." He said: "He would not be able to prevent me!" He said: "You and that."

It is also said that a group of the noble Arabs went with Abd al-Muttalib, and they offered Abraha a third of the wealth of Tihamah on condition that he turn back from the House, but he refused them. Abraha returned to Abd al-Muttalib his camels. Abd al-Muttalib returned to the Quraysh and ordered them to leave Mecca and take refuge on the mountaintops, out of fear for them from the harm of the army. Then Abd al-Muttalib stood, took hold of the ring of the door of the Ka'bah, and with him stood a group of the Quraysh, calling upon Allah and seeking His help against Abraha and his army. Abd al-Muttalib said, while holding the ring of the door of the Ka'bah:

"O Allah, indeed a man defends his camp,
So defend Your sanctuary.
Let their cross not overcome
And their stratagem against Your might, tomorrow, not prevail."

Ibn Ishaq said: Then Abd al-Muttalib released the ring of the door, and they went out to the mountaintops [[See: al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah of Ibn Hisham (1/52).]].

Muqatil ibn Sulayman mentioned that they left near the House a hundred garlanded camels, perhaps some of the army would take something from them unjustly, and Allah would take vengeance on him.

When Abraha woke in the morning, he prepared to enter Mecca. He readied his elephant, which was named Mahmud, and arrayed his army. When they turned the elephant towards Mecca, Nufayl ibn Habib came and stood beside it, then took hold of its ear and said: "Kneel down, Mahmud, and return safely from where you came, for you are in the land of Allah the Sacred." Then he let go of its ear, and the elephant knelt down. Nufayl ibn Habib ran off until he climbed up the mountain. They struck the elephant to make it stand, but it refused. They struck it on the head with an iron implement and inserted their hooks into its flanks and pricked it with them to make it stand, but it refused. They turned it back towards Yemen and it got up and trotted; they turned it towards Syria and it did the same; they turned it towards the east and it did the same; and when they turned it towards Mecca it knelt down. Allah sent upon them birds from the sea, like swallows and sparrows. With each bird were three stones it carried: one stone in its beak and two in its feet, like chickpeas and lentils. They did not strike any of them without destroying them, though not all of them were struck. They fled in all directions, rushing along the road and asking about Nufayl to guide them along this path. Nufayl was on the top of the mountain with the Quraysh and the Arabs of the Hijaz, looking at what vengeance Allah had sent upon the People of the Elephant. Nufayl kept saying: "Where is the escape? The God is the Seeker, and the Ashram is the defeated, not the victor."

Ibn Ishaq said: Nufayl also said in this:

"Ah, may Rudayna greet us, may our eyes be bright at dawn,
Rudayna, if you had seen, and you did not see, by the side of al-Muhassab, what we saw,
Then you would have excused me and praised my course, and you would not have grieved over what had passed between us.
I praised Allah when I saw the birds, and feared the stones that would be thrown upon us.
Every people asks about Nufayl, as if I owed a debt to the Habashah!"

After it is related, with its chains of transmission, that Al-Waqidi said: when they had prepared themselves to enter the Haram (the Sacred Precinct of Makkah) and had readied the elephant, they could not turn it toward any direction other than the Haram, but whichever direction they turned it, it went. When they turned it toward the Haram, it knelt down and cried out. Abraha began to attack the elephant's handler, shouting at him and beating him, so as to force the elephant to enter the Haram. The matter dragged on.

Meanwhile, Abd al-Muttalib and a group of the nobles of Makkah, among them al-Mut'im ibn 'Adi, 'Amr ibn 'A'idh ibn 'Imran ibn Makhzum, and Mas'ud [ibn 'Amr] al-Thaqafi, were on Hira' watching what the Abyssinians were doing and what would befall them concerning the matter of the elephant, which was a wondrous and marvellous thing. While they were in this state, Allah sent against them birds in flocks (ababil), meaning in separate groups, yellow, unlike pigeons, with red feet. Each bird carried three stones. They came and hovered over them and released those stones upon them, and they were destroyed.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: They brought two elephants. One of them, Mahmud, knelt down, while the other became obstinate and was pelted with stones.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: They had a number of elephants with them. Mahmud, which was the king's elephant, knelt down so that the rest of the elephants would follow its example. Among them was an elephant that became obstinate and was pelted, and the rest of the elephants then fled.

'Ata' ibn Yasar and others said: Not all of them were struck by the punishment at that very moment. Some of them perished swiftly, and some began to fall apart limb by limb while they were fleeing. Abraha was among those who fell apart limb by limb, until he died in the lands of Khath'am.

Ibn Ishaq said: They set out, falling apart along every road and perishing at every watering place. Abraha was afflicted in his body, and they carried him with them, while his fingers dropped off one joint at a time, until they brought him to Sana'a, and he was like a young bird. He did not die until his chest split open from his heart, so they claim.

Muqatil ibn Sulayman mentioned that the Quraysh obtained a great deal of wealth from their spoils and from what was with them, and that Abd al-Muttalib that day acquired so much gold that it filled a pit.

Ibn Ishaq said: Ya'qub ibn 'Utba informed me that it was related to him that the first time measles and smallpox were seen in the land of the Arabs was in that year, and that the first time bitter herbs, colocynth, and 'ushr [a bitter plant] were seen was also that year.

[Editor's note: see Ibn Hisham's Sirah (1/54).]

The same is related from 'Ikrimah, through a sound route.

Ibn Ishaq said: When Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ), among the blessings and favours He reminded the Quraysh of was what He had averted from them of the affair of the Abyssinians, so that their affairs and their period [of prosperity] might endure. He said: ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant? Did He not make their plot go astray? And He sent against them birds in flocks, striking them with stones of baked clay, and He made them like chewed-up straw.﴾ ﴿For the security of the Quraysh, their security in the caravans of winter and summer, let them worship the Lord of this House, who has fed them against hunger and secured them against fear.﴾ [Surah Quraysh]. That is, so that He would not change anything of their condition in which they were, because of the good Allah wished for them, had they accepted it.

Ibn Hisham said: The ababil are groups, and the Arabs do not use a singular form for them. He said: As for sijjil, Yunus the grammarian and Abu 'Ubayda informed me that among the Arabs it means "hard and firm." He said: Some of the exegetes mentioned that they are two words in Persian, which the Arabs made into one word; it is actually sanj and gil. By sanj is meant stone, and by gil, clay. The meaning is: stones of these two kinds, stone and clay. He said: The 'asf is the leaf of the crop that has not been cut, its singular being 'asfah. End of what he mentioned.

[Editor's note: see Ibn Hisham's Sirah (1/55).]

Hammad ibn Salamah related from 'Asim, from Zirr, from 'Abd Allah, and Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, regarding ﴿birds in flocks﴾ that he said: "al-Faraq" [the separate groups].

Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: ababil means that some of them follow others. Al-Hasan al-Basri and Qatadah said: ababil means many. Mujahid said: ababil means scattered, consecutive, and gathered together. Ibn Zayd said: ababil means varied, coming from here and from there; they came to them from every place.

Al-Kisa'i said: I heard the grammarians saying: ubul is like 'ujul [calves]. He said: I have also heard some grammarians say: the singular of ababil is ibil.

Ibn Jarir said: [Ibn al-Muthanna related to us]: 'Abd al-A'la related to me, Dawud related to me, from Ishaq ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith ibn Nawfal, that he said regarding His saying ﴿and He sent against them birds in flocks﴾: they are groups, like herds of camels.

Abu Kurayb related to us: Waki' related to us, from Ibn 'Awn, from Ibn Sirin, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿and He sent against them birds in flocks﴾ that he said: They had beaks like the beaks of birds and paws like the paws of dogs.

Ya'qub related to us: Hushaym related to us: Husayn informed us, from 'Ikrimah regarding His saying ﴿birds in flocks﴾ that he said: They were green birds that came out of the sea, having heads like the heads of beasts of prey.

Ibn Bashshar related to us: Ibn Mahdi related to us, from Sufyan, from al-A'mash, from Abu Sufyan, from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr regarding ﴿birds in flocks﴾ that he said: They are sea birds, black, with stones in their beaks and talons.

These are sound chains of transmission.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: They were green birds with yellow beaks, moving among them.

From Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and 'Ata': the ababil birds were like those called the mythical "'Anqa' Mughrib." This was related from them by Ibn Abi Hatim.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: Abu Zur'ah related to us: 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Shaybah related to us: Abu Mu'awiyah related to us, from al-A'mash, from Abu Sufyan, from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, who said: When Allah wished to destroy the companions of the elephant, He sent against them birds created from the sea, like swallows. Each bird carried three stones, speckled: two stones in its feet and one stone in its beak. He said: They came and lined up over their heads, then they screamed and dropped what was in their feet and beaks. No stone fell on a man's head without coming out of his anus, and none fell on any part of his body without coming out the other side. Allah sent a strong wind that struck the stones and increased their force, and they were all destroyed.

As for al-Suddi, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿stones of baked clay﴾: he said: clay in stones, "sank wa-kil" [two Persian words for stone and clay]. We have already presented the explanation of this, which suffices here without repetition.

* *

As for His saying ﴿and He made them like chewed-up straw﴾: Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it means the chaff that common people call hubur. In another report from Sa'id: the leaves of wheat. He also said: the 'asf is chaff, and al-ma'kul is the young green crop cut for animals. Al-Hasan al-Basri said the same.

From Ibn 'Abbas: the 'asf is the husk that is over the grain, like the covering over wheat.

Ibn Zayd said: the 'asf is the leaves of the crop and the leaves of herbs when animals eat them and then drop them as dung, and it becomes crumbled.

The meaning is: Allah, glorified and exalted, destroyed them and annihilated them, and turned them back with their scheming and their rage, without gaining any good. He destroyed most of them, and none of them returned with anything good except wounded, as happened to their king Abraha, whose chest split open from his heart when he reached his city of Sana'a. He informed them of what had happened to them, and then he died. His son Yaksum then ruled after him, then after him his brother Masruq ibn Abraha [ruled].

[Editor's note: see Ibn Hisham's Sirah (1/61–62).]

Then Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan al-Himyari went to Khosrow [the Persian king] seeking his help against the Abyssinians, and he sent with him troops from his armies, who fought alongside him. Allah restored to them their kingdom and what their forefathers had possessed of kingship, and delegations of the Arabs came to him to congratulate him.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr related to us, from 'Amrah bint 'Abd al-Rahman ibn As'ad ibn Zurarah, from 'A'ishah, who said: I saw the elephant's driver and its handler in Makkah, both blind and crippled, begging for food.

[Editor's note: see Ibn Hisham's Sirah (1/57).] Al-Waqidi related the same from 'A'ishah, and he also related from Asma' bint Abi Bakr that she said: they were both crippled, begging people for food, near Isaf and Na'ilah, where the polytheists slaughter their sacrifices.

I say: the name of the elephant's driver was Unays.

The hafiz Abu Nu'aym mentioned in his book Dala'il al-Nubuwwah, through the route of Ibn Wahb, from Ibn Lahi'ah, from 'Uqayl ibn Khalid, from 'Uthman ibn al-Mughirah, the story of the companions of the elephant. He did not mention that Abraha came from Yemen, but rather that he appointed over the army a man called Shamar ibn Maksud, and the army was twenty thousand strong. He mentioned that the birds attacked them at night, and in the morning they were lying dead.

This narrative is very strange, although Abu Nu'aym strengthened it and preferred it over others. The correct account is that Abraha al-Ashram al-Habashi came to Makkah, as the narratives and the poetry indicate. Likewise Ibn Lahi'ah related from al-Aswad, from 'Urwah, that Abraha sent al-Aswad ibn Maksud over a battalion with the elephant, and he did not mention Abraha's own coming. The correct view is that he came, and perhaps Ibn Maksud was at the head of the army. And Allah knows best.

Then Ibn Ishaq related some of the poetry of the Arabs concerning the story of the companions of the elephant. Among it is the poetry of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Za'bari:

They drew back from the heart of Makkah, for it
Was of old a sanctuary never to be violated...
The Shi'ra [star] was not created on the nights it was made sacred,
When no mighty one among mankind would seek it...
Ask the commander of the army what he saw of it?
For he will surely be told of its fate by the ignorant...
Sixty thousand did not return to their land,
Nor did the sick among them survive after their return...
'Ad and Jurhum had dwelt there before them,
And Allah above His servants keeps it secure...

[Editor's note: see Ibn Hisham's Sirah (1/58).]

Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat al-Ansari al-Mari [in some copies: al-Madani] said:
And of their doing on the day of the elephant of al-Habush,
When everything they brought was a cluster of crowded ones...
Their goads beneath its flanks,
And they had slit its nose, so it was torn...
They made its whip a lash,
When they turned it, its back was wounded...
So it turned back, retreating along its path,
And whoever was there had earned injustice...
Then He sent upon them from above a stone-storm
That wrapped them up like a sack of ... [a crowd]...
Their rabbis urged them to patience,
While they bleated like the bleating of sheep...

Abu al-Salt ibn Abi Rabi'ah al-Thaqafi said, and it is also attributed to Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt ibn Abi Rabi'ah:
Indeed the signs of our Lord are lasting,
None disputes them except the ungrateful...
The night and the day were created, and each
Has a reckoning that is clear and decreed...
Then a merciful Lord reveals the day
With a sun whose rays are spread out...
The elephant was held back at al-Mughammas until
It began to crawl, as if it were struck down...
Its neck was bound to the ground, as if it had been cut
From the back of a steep hill...
Around it were champions of the kings of Kindah,
Hard in war, like falcons...
They left it behind, then all of them fled,
All their shin bones broken.

Every religion on the Day of Resurrection with Allah ... is ruined, except the religion of the Hanifiyyah (the pure monotheism of Abraham) ...

I have already mentioned in the commentary on Surah al-Fath that on the day of al-Hudaybiyyah, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came into view at the mountain pass that descends to the Quraysh, his camel knelt down. They urged her on, but she refused to rise. They said, "al-Qaswa has become stubborn," meaning she had balked. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "al-Qaswa has not become stubborn, nor is that her habit, but the one who restrained the elephant has restrained her." Then he said, "By Him in whose hand is my soul, they will not ask me today for any arrangement in which they honour the sacred things of Allah, except that I will agree to it." Then he urged her on and she got up. The hadith is related by al-Bukhari alone [[The takhrij of this hadith was mentioned under the commentary on verse 26 of Surah al-Fath, and it is in Sahih al-Bukhari, nos. (2731, 2732).]].

In the two Sahihs (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim) it is reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said on the day of the Conquest of Makkah: "Allah withheld the elephant from Makkah and gave His Messenger and the believers power over it. Its sanctity has returned today as it was yesterday. So let the one who is present convey it to the one who is absent" [[Sahih al-Bukhari, no. (112), and Sahih Muslim, no. (1355), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]].

End of the commentary on Surah al-Fil.

Commentary of Ibn Kathir (Tafsir al-Quran al-'Azim) on surah 105, verse 1–5 (part 1 of 3):

Tafsir of Surat al-Fil (The Elephant)
It is a Meccan surah.
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
* *
This is one of the blessings with which Allah favoured the Quraysh, in that He turned away from them the People of the Elephant, who had resolved to demolish the Ka'bah and erase its trace from existence. So Allah destroyed them, humbled their noses, frustrated their endeavour, misguided their deeds, and returned them in the worst state of failure. They were a Christian people, and their religion at that time was closer to the truth than the idol worship in which the Quraysh were engaged. Yet this was by way of irhas (a preparatory sign) and tawti'ah (a paving of the way) for the mission of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for he was born in that year according to the most well-known opinions. The state of the decree (qadar) seems to say: "We did not give you victory, O assembly of Quraysh, over the Abyssinians because of your superiority over them, but to protect the Ancient House, which We will honour, exalt and revere through the mission of the unlettered Prophet Muhammad, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, the Seal of the Prophets."

This is the story of the People of the Elephant in a summarised, concise and brief manner. It has already been mentioned in the story of the People of the Trench (ukhdud) [[At the commentary on verse 4 of Surat al-Buruj.]] that Dhu Nuwas, who was the last of the kings of Himyar and was a polytheist, was the one who killed the People of the Trench, who were Christians, and they numbered nearly twenty thousand. None of them escaped except Dawas Dhu Tha'labān, who went and sought help from Caesar, the king of Syria, who was a Christian. He wrote to the Negus, the king of Abyssinia, on his behalf, since he was closer to them. So he sent with him two commanders: Ariyat and Abraha ibn al-Sabbah, Abu Yaksum [[In the manuscript A: "Abu Bakshum".]], with a dense army. They entered Yemen, roamed through its lands, and seized the kingdom from Himyar, and Dhu Nuwas perished by drowning in the sea. The Abyssinians established their rule over Yemen, and these two commanders were over them: Ariyat and Abraha. They disagreed about their affairs, contended, fought and drew up their lines against each other. One of them said to the other: "There is no need for the two armies to clash between us, but come out to me and I will come out to you. Whichever of us kills the other will then hold the kingdom alone." The other agreed to that, and they fought in single combat, each holding a spear. Ariyat charged at Abraha and struck him with the sword, slitting his nose and mouth and splitting his face. Atwadah, the mawla of Abraha, charged at Ariyat and killed him, and Abraha returned wounded. He treated his wound and it healed, and he took sole charge of the Abyssinian army in Yemen. The Negus wrote to him rebuking him for what he had done, threatening him and swearing that he would certainly trample his land and cut off his forelock. Abraha sent to him seeking to soften his heart and to win him over, and he sent with his messenger gifts and presents, and a leather bag containing soil from Yemen, and he had cut off his forelock and sent it with him. He wrote in his letter: "Let the king tread upon this bag so that he may fulfil his oath, and this is my forelock, which I have sent to you." When that reached him, it pleased him, he was content with him, and he confirmed him in his post. Abraha sent to the Negus saying: "I will build for you a church in the land of Yemen, the like of which has never been built before." So he began to build a vast church in San'a, high in its construction, lofty in its courtyard, and adorned in its surroundings. The Arabs named it al-Qulleys because of its height, for the one who looks at it nearly has his cap fall from his head because of the height of its building. Abraha al-Ashram resolved to divert the Hajj of the Arabs to it, just as the Hajj is performed to the Ka'bah in Mecca, and he proclaimed this throughout his kingdom. The Arabs, both the 'Adnani and the Qahtani, disliked that, and the Quraysh were greatly angered by it, to the extent that some of them went to it and managed to enter it by night. They defiled it and then returned. When the custodians (sadanah) saw that act of defilement, they reported the matter to their king Abraha and said to him: "Only some of the Quraysh did this, out of anger for their House which you have sought to rival with this one." So Abraha swore that he would certainly march to the House in Mecca and destroy it stone by stone.

Muqatil ibn Sulayman mentioned that some young men of the Quraysh entered it and kindled a fire inside it, and on a day when there was a strong wind, the fire spread and burnt it, and it collapsed to the ground.

So Abraha prepared himself for this, and set out with a dense, mighty army, so that no one could repel him from it. He took with him a great elephant of enormous body, the like of which had never been seen, called Mahmud, which the Negus, king of Abyssinia, had sent to him for this purpose. It is said that there were also eight elephants with him, and it is said twelve elephants, and other figures were said, and Allah knows best. He intended to demolish the Ka'bah with it, by placing chains on the corners and putting them round the elephant's neck, then driving it so that it would knock down the wall all at once. When the Arabs heard of his march, they were greatly alarmed, and they considered it their duty to defend the House and to repel whoever intended to harm it with evil. A man from the nobles and kings of the people of Yemen, called "Dhu Nafr," went out to him and called his people and whoever among the other Arabs answered him to fight Abraha and to strive in the cause of the House of Allah, against what he intended of its demolition and ruin. They responded to him and fought Abraha, but he defeated them, because of what Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, willed of the honour and exaltation of the House. Dhu Nafr was captured and Abraha kept him with him. Then he proceeded on his way until, when he reached the land of Khath'am, Nufayl ibn Habib al-Khath'ami confronted him with his people, Shahran and Nahis, and they fought him, but Abraha defeated them, and Nufayl ibn Habib was captured. He intended to kill him, then pardoned him, and kept him with him to guide him through the lands of the Hijaz. When he drew near the land of al-Ta'if, its people, Thaqif, came out to him and gave him gifts out of fear for their House that they had there, which they called al-Lat. So he honoured them, and they sent with him Abu Righal as a guide. When Abraha reached al-Mughammas, which is near Mecca, he halted there, and his army raided the camels and other livestock of the people of Mecca, and they seized them. Among the herd were two hundred camels belonging to Abd al-Muttalib. The one who raided the herd on Abraha's orders was the commander of the vanguard, who was called "al-Aswad ibn Maqsud." Some of the Arabs satirised him, as reported by Ibn Ishaq [[See: al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah of Ibn Hisham (1/51).]]. Abraha sent Hunatah al-Himyari to Mecca and ordered him to bring him the noblest of the Quraysh, and to inform them that the king had not come to fight them unless they tried to repel him from the House. Hunatah came and was directed to Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim, and he conveyed to him what Abraha had said. Abd al-Muttalib said to him: "By Allah, we do not wish to fight him, and we have no power for that. This is the Sacred House of Allah and the House of His friend Abraham. If He protects it from him, then it is His House and His sanctuary, and if He leaves him to it, then by Allah we have no defence against him." Hunatah said to him: "Then go with me to him." So he went with him, and when Abraha saw him he held him in great honour, for Abd al-Muttalib was a handsome man of fine appearance. Abraha got down from his throne and sat with him on the carpet, and said to his interpreter: "Say to him: What is your need?" Abd al-Muttalib said to the interpreter: "My need is that the king return to me the two hundred camels that he has taken from me." Abraha said to his interpreter: "Say to him: You had impressed me when I saw you, but now I have lost my regard for you since you spoke to me. Do you speak to me about two hundred camels that I have taken from you, and leave aside a House which is your religion and the religion of your fathers, and which I have come to demolish, and you do not speak to me about it?" Abd al-Muttalib said to him: "I am the lord of the camels, and the House has a Lord who will protect it." He said: "He would not be able to prevent me!" He said: "You and that."

It is also said that a group of the noble Arabs went with Abd al-Muttalib, and they offered Abraha a third of the wealth of Tihamah on condition that he turn back from the House, but he refused them. Abraha returned to Abd al-Muttalib his camels. Abd al-Muttalib returned to the Quraysh and ordered them to leave Mecca and take refuge on the mountaintops, out of fear for them from the harm of the army. Then Abd al-Muttalib stood, took hold of the ring of the door of the Ka'bah, and with him stood a group of the Quraysh, calling upon Allah and seeking His help against Abraha and his army. Abd al-Muttalib said, while holding the ring of the door of the Ka'bah:

"O Allah, indeed a man defends his camp,
So defend Your sanctuary.
Let their cross not overcome
And their stratagem against Your might, tomorrow, not prevail."

Ibn Ishaq said: Then Abd al-Muttalib released the ring of the door, and they went out to the mountaintops [[See: al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah of Ibn Hisham (1/52).]].

Muqatil ibn Sulayman mentioned that they left near the House a hundred garlanded camels, perhaps some of the army would take something from them unjustly, and Allah would take vengeance on him.

When Abraha woke in the morning, he prepared to enter Mecca. He readied his elephant, which was named Mahmud, and arrayed his army. When they turned the elephant towards Mecca, Nufayl ibn Habib came and stood beside it, then took hold of its ear and said: "Kneel down, Mahmud, and return safely from where you came, for you are in the land of Allah the Sacred." Then he let go of its ear, and the elephant knelt down. Nufayl ibn Habib ran off until he climbed up the mountain. They struck the elephant to make it stand, but it refused. They struck it on the head with an iron implement and inserted their hooks into its flanks and pricked it with them to make it stand, but it refused. They turned it back towards Yemen and it got up and trotted; they turned it towards Syria and it did the same; they turned it towards the east and it did the same; and when they turned it towards Mecca it knelt down. Allah sent upon them birds from the sea, like swallows and sparrows. With each bird were three stones it carried: one stone in its beak and two in its feet, like chickpeas and lentils. They did not strike any of them without destroying them, though not all of them were struck. They fled in all directions, rushing along the road and asking about Nufayl to guide them along this path. Nufayl was on the top of the mountain with the Quraysh and the Arabs of the Hijaz, looking at what vengeance Allah had sent upon the People of the Elephant. Nufayl kept saying: "Where is the escape? The God is the Seeker, and the Ashram is the defeated, not the victor."

Ibn Ishaq said: Nufayl also said in this:

"Ah, may Rudayna greet us, may our eyes be bright at dawn,
Rudayna, if you had seen, and you did not see, by the side of al-Muhassab, what we saw,
Then you would have excused me and praised my course, and you would not have grieved over what had passed between us.
I praised Allah when I saw the birds, and feared the stones that would be thrown upon us.
Every people asks about Nufayl, as if I owed a debt to the Habashah!"

After it is related, with its chains of transmission, that Al-Waqidi said: when they had prepared themselves to enter the Haram (the Sacred Precinct of Makkah) and had readied the elephant, they could not turn it toward any direction other than the Haram, but whichever direction they turned it, it went. When they turned it toward the Haram, it knelt down and cried out. Abraha began to attack the elephant's handler, shouting at him and beating him, so as to force the elephant to enter the Haram. The matter dragged on.

Meanwhile, Abd al-Muttalib and a group of the nobles of Makkah, among them al-Mut'im ibn 'Adi, 'Amr ibn 'A'idh ibn 'Imran ibn Makhzum, and Mas'ud [ibn 'Amr] al-Thaqafi, were on Hira' watching what the Abyssinians were doing and what would befall them concerning the matter of the elephant, which was a wondrous and marvellous thing. While they were in this state, Allah sent against them birds in flocks (ababil), meaning in separate groups, yellow, unlike pigeons, with red feet. Each bird carried three stones. They came and hovered over them and released those stones upon them, and they were destroyed.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: They brought two elephants. One of them, Mahmud, knelt down, while the other became obstinate and was pelted with stones.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: They had a number of elephants with them. Mahmud, which was the king's elephant, knelt down so that the rest of the elephants would follow its example. Among them was an elephant that became obstinate and was pelted, and the rest of the elephants then fled.

'Ata' ibn Yasar and others said: Not all of them were struck by the punishment at that very moment. Some of them perished swiftly, and some began to fall apart limb by limb while they were fleeing. Abraha was among those who fell apart limb by limb, until he died in the lands of Khath'am.

Ibn Ishaq said: They set out, falling apart along every road and perishing at every watering place. Abraha was afflicted in his body, and they carried him with them, while his fingers dropped off one joint at a time, until they brought him to Sana'a, and he was like a young bird. He did not die until his chest split open from his heart, so they claim.

Muqatil ibn Sulayman mentioned that the Quraysh obtained a great deal of wealth from their spoils and from what was with them, and that Abd al-Muttalib that day acquired so much gold that it filled a pit.

Ibn Ishaq said: Ya'qub ibn 'Utba informed me that it was related to him that the first time measles and smallpox were seen in the land of the Arabs was in that year, and that the first time bitter herbs, colocynth, and 'ushr [a bitter plant] were seen was also that year.

[Editor's note: see Ibn Hisham's Sirah (1/54).]

The same is related from 'Ikrimah, through a sound route.

Ibn Ishaq said: When Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ), among the blessings and favours He reminded the Quraysh of was what He had averted from them of the affair of the Abyssinians, so that their affairs and their period [of prosperity] might endure. He said: ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant? Did He not make their plot go astray? And He sent against them birds in flocks, striking them with stones of baked clay, and He made them like chewed-up straw.﴾ ﴿For the security of the Quraysh, their security in the caravans of winter and summer, let them worship the Lord of this House, who has fed them against hunger and secured them against fear.﴾ [Surah Quraysh]. That is, so that He would not change anything of their condition in which they were, because of the good Allah wished for them, had they accepted it.

Ibn Hisham said: The ababil are groups, and the Arabs do not use a singular form for them. He said: As for sijjil, Yunus the grammarian and Abu 'Ubayda informed me that among the Arabs it means "hard and firm." He said: Some of the exegetes mentioned that they are two words in Persian, which the Arabs made into one word; it is actually sanj and gil. By sanj is meant stone, and by gil, clay. The meaning is: stones of these two kinds, stone and clay. He said: The 'asf is the leaf of the crop that has not been cut, its singular being 'asfah. End of what he mentioned.

[Editor's note: see Ibn Hisham's Sirah (1/55).]

Hammad ibn Salamah related from 'Asim, from Zirr, from 'Abd Allah, and Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, regarding ﴿birds in flocks﴾ that he said: "al-Faraq" [the separate groups].

Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: ababil means that some of them follow others. Al-Hasan al-Basri and Qatadah said: ababil means many. Mujahid said: ababil means scattered, consecutive, and gathered together. Ibn Zayd said: ababil means varied, coming from here and from there; they came to them from every place.

Al-Kisa'i said: I heard the grammarians saying: ubul is like 'ujul [calves]. He said: I have also heard some grammarians say: the singular of ababil is ibil.

Ibn Jarir said: [Ibn al-Muthanna related to us]: 'Abd al-A'la related to me, Dawud related to me, from Ishaq ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith ibn Nawfal, that he said regarding His saying ﴿and He sent against them birds in flocks﴾: they are groups, like herds of camels.

Abu Kurayb related to us: Waki' related to us, from Ibn 'Awn, from Ibn Sirin, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿and He sent against them birds in flocks﴾ that he said: They had beaks like the beaks of birds and paws like the paws of dogs.

Ya'qub related to us: Hushaym related to us: Husayn informed us, from 'Ikrimah regarding His saying ﴿birds in flocks﴾ that he said: They were green birds that came out of the sea, having heads like the heads of beasts of prey.

Ibn Bashshar related to us: Ibn Mahdi related to us, from Sufyan, from al-A'mash, from Abu Sufyan, from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr regarding ﴿birds in flocks﴾ that he said: They are sea birds, black, with stones in their beaks and talons.

These are sound chains of transmission.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: They were green birds with yellow beaks, moving among them.

From Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and 'Ata': the ababil birds were like those called the mythical "'Anqa' Mughrib." This was related from them by Ibn Abi Hatim.

Ibn Abi Hatim said: Abu Zur'ah related to us: 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Shaybah related to us: Abu Mu'awiyah related to us, from al-A'mash, from Abu Sufyan, from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, who said: When Allah wished to destroy the companions of the elephant, He sent against them birds created from the sea, like swallows. Each bird carried three stones, speckled: two stones in its feet and one stone in its beak. He said: They came and lined up over their heads, then they screamed and dropped what was in their feet and beaks. No stone fell on a man's head without coming out of his anus, and none fell on any part of his body without coming out the other side. Allah sent a strong wind that struck the stones and increased their force, and they were all destroyed.

As for al-Suddi, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿stones of baked clay﴾: he said: clay in stones, "sank wa-kil" [two Persian words for stone and clay]. We have already presented the explanation of this, which suffices here without repetition.

* *

As for His saying ﴿and He made them like chewed-up straw﴾: Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it means the chaff that common people call hubur. In another report from Sa'id: the leaves of wheat. He also said: the 'asf is chaff, and al-ma'kul is the young green crop cut for animals. Al-Hasan al-Basri said the same.

From Ibn 'Abbas: the 'asf is the husk that is over the grain, like the covering over wheat.

Ibn Zayd said: the 'asf is the leaves of the crop and the leaves of herbs when animals eat them and then drop them as dung, and it becomes crumbled.

The meaning is: Allah, glorified and exalted, destroyed them and annihilated them, and turned them back with their scheming and their rage, without gaining any good. He destroyed most of them, and none of them returned with anything good except wounded, as happened to their king Abraha, whose chest split open from his heart when he reached his city of Sana'a. He informed them of what had happened to them, and then he died. His son Yaksum then ruled after him, then after him his brother Masruq ibn Abraha [ruled].

[Editor's note: see Ibn Hisham's Sirah (1/61–62).]

Then Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan al-Himyari went to Khosrow [the Persian king] seeking his help against the Abyssinians, and he sent with him troops from his armies, who fought alongside him. Allah restored to them their kingdom and what their forefathers had possessed of kingship, and delegations of the Arabs came to him to congratulate him.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr related to us, from 'Amrah bint 'Abd al-Rahman ibn As'ad ibn Zurarah, from 'A'ishah, who said: I saw the elephant's driver and its handler in Makkah, both blind and crippled, begging for food.

[Editor's note: see Ibn Hisham's Sirah (1/57).] Al-Waqidi related the same from 'A'ishah, and he also related from Asma' bint Abi Bakr that she said: they were both crippled, begging people for food, near Isaf and Na'ilah, where the polytheists slaughter their sacrifices.

I say: the name of the elephant's driver was Unays.

The hafiz Abu Nu'aym mentioned in his book Dala'il al-Nubuwwah, through the route of Ibn Wahb, from Ibn Lahi'ah, from 'Uqayl ibn Khalid, from 'Uthman ibn al-Mughirah, the story of the companions of the elephant. He did not mention that Abraha came from Yemen, but rather that he appointed over the army a man called Shamar ibn Maksud, and the army was twenty thousand strong. He mentioned that the birds attacked them at night, and in the morning they were lying dead.

This narrative is very strange, although Abu Nu'aym strengthened it and preferred it over others. The correct account is that Abraha al-Ashram al-Habashi came to Makkah, as the narratives and the poetry indicate. Likewise Ibn Lahi'ah related from al-Aswad, from 'Urwah, that Abraha sent al-Aswad ibn Maksud over a battalion with the elephant, and he did not mention Abraha's own coming. The correct view is that he came, and perhaps Ibn Maksud was at the head of the army. And Allah knows best.

Then Ibn Ishaq related some of the poetry of the Arabs concerning the story of the companions of the elephant. Among it is the poetry of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Za'bari:

They drew back from the heart of Makkah, for it
Was of old a sanctuary never to be violated...
The Shi'ra [star] was not created on the nights it was made sacred,
When no mighty one among mankind would seek it...
Ask the commander of the army what he saw of it?
For he will surely be told of its fate by the ignorant...
Sixty thousand did not return to their land,
Nor did the sick among them survive after their return...
'Ad and Jurhum had dwelt there before them,
And Allah above His servants keeps it secure...

[Editor's note: see Ibn Hisham's Sirah (1/58).]

Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat al-Ansari al-Mari [in some copies: al-Madani] said:
And of their doing on the day of the elephant of al-Habush,
When everything they brought was a cluster of crowded ones...
Their goads beneath its flanks,
And they had slit its nose, so it was torn...
They made its whip a lash,
When they turned it, its back was wounded...
So it turned back, retreating along its path,
And whoever was there had earned injustice...
Then He sent upon them from above a stone-storm
That wrapped them up like a sack of ... [a crowd]...
Their rabbis urged them to patience,
While they bleated like the bleating of sheep...

Abu al-Salt ibn Abi Rabi'ah al-Thaqafi said, and it is also attributed to Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt ibn Abi Rabi'ah:
Indeed the signs of our Lord are lasting,
None disputes them except the ungrateful...
The night and the day were created, and each
Has a reckoning that is clear and decreed...
Then a merciful Lord reveals the day
With a sun whose rays are spread out...
The elephant was held back at al-Mughammas until
It began to crawl, as if it were struck down...
Its neck was bound to the ground, as if it had been cut
From the back of a steep hill...
Around it were champions of the kings of Kindah,
Hard in war, like falcons...
They left it behind, then all of them fled,
All their shin bones broken.

Every religion on the Day of Resurrection with Allah ... is ruined, except the religion of the Hanifiyyah (the pure monotheism of Abraham) ...

I have already mentioned in the commentary on Surah al-Fath that on the day of al-Hudaybiyyah, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came into view at the mountain pass that descends to the Quraysh, his camel knelt down. They urged her on, but she refused to rise. They said, "al-Qaswa has become stubborn," meaning she had balked. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "al-Qaswa has not become stubborn, nor is that her habit, but the one who restrained the elephant has restrained her." Then he said, "By Him in whose hand is my soul, they will not ask me today for any arrangement in which they honour the sacred things of Allah, except that I will agree to it." Then he urged her on and she got up. The hadith is related by al-Bukhari alone [[The takhrij of this hadith was mentioned under the commentary on verse 26 of Surah al-Fath, and it is in Sahih al-Bukhari, nos. (2731, 2732).]].

In the two Sahihs (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim) it is reported that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said on the day of the Conquest of Makkah: "Allah withheld the elephant from Makkah and gave His Messenger and the believers power over it. Its sanctity has returned today as it was yesterday. So let the one who is present convey it to the one who is absent" [[Sahih al-Bukhari, no. (112), and Sahih Muslim, no. (1355), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]].

End of the commentary on Surah al-Fil.

Commentary of Ibn Kathir (Tafsir al-Quran al-'Azim) on surah 105, verse 1–5 (part 1 of 3):

Tafsir of Surat al-Fil (The Elephant)
It is a Meccan surah.
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
* *
This is one of the blessings with which Allah favoured the Quraysh, in that He turned away from them the People of the Elephant, who had resolved to demolish the Ka'bah and erase its trace from existence. So Allah destroyed them, humbled their noses, frustrated their endeavour, misguided their deeds, and returned them in the worst state of failure. They were a Christian people, and their religion at that time was closer to the truth than the idol worship in which the Quraysh were engaged. Yet this was by way of irhas (a preparatory sign) and tawti'ah (a paving of the way) for the mission of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for he was born in that year according to the most well-known opinions. The state of the decree (qadar) seems to say: "We did not give you victory, O assembly of Quraysh, over the Abyssinians because of your superiority over them, but to protect the Ancient House, which We will honour, exalt and revere through the mission of the unlettered Prophet Muhammad, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, the Seal of the Prophets."

This is the story of the People of the Elephant in a summarised, concise and brief manner. It has already been mentioned in the story of the People of the Trench (ukhdud) [[At the commentary on verse 4 of Surat al-Buruj.]] that Dhu Nuwas, who was the last of the kings of Himyar and was a polytheist, was the one who killed the People of the Trench, who were Christians, and they numbered nearly twenty thousand. None of them escaped except Dawas Dhu Tha'labān, who went and sought help from Caesar, the king of Syria, who was a Christian. He wrote to the Negus, the king of Abyssinia, on his behalf, since he was closer to them. So he sent with him two commanders: Ariyat and Abraha ibn al-Sabbah, Abu Yaksum [[In the manuscript A: "Abu Bakshum".]], with a dense army. They entered Yemen, roamed through its lands, and seized the kingdom from Himyar, and Dhu Nuwas perished by drowning in the sea. The Abyssinians established their rule over Yemen, and these two commanders were over them: Ariyat and Abraha. They disagreed about their affairs, contended, fought and drew up their lines against each other.
